heroLead: North Johns is a small community in the Warrior area of Jefferson County, where mineral interests tend to be modest fractions passed down within a handful of extended families rather than large corporate-held blocks.
intro: In a place this small, the mineral ownership picture usually comes down to a few interconnected families whose ancestors farmed or worked coal in the area a century ago. Interests here are often tiny on paper — a sixteenth, a thirty-second — but that doesn't mean they're not worth pursuing, especially if the tract sits inside a producing coalbed methane unit that's been paying royalties for years without the current owner realizing how the fraction adds up.

sections.heading: Small Fractions Add Up Differently Than People Expect
paragraphs: A tiny fractional interest in an active, well-performing unit can be worth more than a much larger fraction in a marginal one. We look at your actual fraction against the unit's real production, rather than the size of the number written on the deed, before we tell you what we'd pay. That comparison is the single biggest reason two families with similar-looking fractions can end up with very different offers.

sections.heading: Confirming Ownership in a Small Community
paragraphs: Because so much of North Johns' land history runs through a small number of families, it's common for a mineral interest to have passed through several informal transfers — a verbal understanding at a funeral, a handshake between cousins — that were never properly recorded. We check the Jefferson County record for what was actually filed and tell you honestly if anything needs to be cleaned up before a sale can close.

faqs.question: Our fraction is very small, like a sixteenth or smaller. Is it worth selling?
faqs.answer: It can be, depending on how the unit it sits in has been performing. We look at the real production numbers rather than dismissing a small fraction outright.

faqs.question: We think there was a verbal agreement between family members that was never put on paper. What now?
faqs.answer: That happens often in small communities like this. We check what's actually recorded and tell you what, if anything, needs to be formalized before we can close.

faqs.question: How do you find out what unit our land is actually in?
faqs.answer: We check state pooling filings against the legal description on your deed. Send us that description and we'll confirm it.

faqs.question: Several of us cousins share the same small fraction. Do we all need to sell together?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Each co-owner can sell their share independently, though we're glad to make one combined offer if the family would rather sell as a group.
